opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core intuition is pretty simple. If the thing you're trying to model is fundamentally physical, why would you want to run it on hardware that's spent decades trying to suppress physics? A digital computer works very hard to make every transistor behave like a clean, deterministic bit. You pay an enormous energy and complexity cost to stamp out noise, fluctuations, and all the natural dynamics of the substrate. Then, on top of that, you turn around and simulate those exact things back in software: stochasticity, diffusion, energy landscapes, equilibration. It's a sort of double tax.

With a physics-based accelerator, you flip that around. You let the hardware's natural dynamics do the computation. If your model is an energy-based model, or something like a diffusion process, or a Langevin-type sampler, those are things physical systems already do natively. A system of coupled oscillators or stochastic circuits relaxing toward equilibrium is, in a very real sense, sampling from a Boltzmann distribution. So the inductive bias of the hardware matches the inductive bias of the model.

And that matters for representation learning specifically. When you want representations that respect physical structure, like symmetries, conservation laws, locality, and the right notion of uncertainty, you want the computational primitives to carry that structure too. Otherwise you're bolting physics onto an architecture as a constraint or a regularizer and hoping gradient descent respects it. If the substrate itself obeys those principles, the representations it learns are going to be shaped by them by default.

There's also the probabilistic angle, which I think is underappreciated. The world at the scales we care about is noisy and uncertain. Physics-informed models really should be generative and probabilistic, capturing distributions over states rather than point estimates. Digital hardware is terrible at generating high-quality randomness efficiently, while thermodynamic hardware gets it essentially for free from thermal fluctuations. So you get orders of magnitude potential gains in energy efficiency for exactly the class of algorithms that I think are most natural for modeling the physical world.

So to me it's a kind of co-design argument. Match the physics of the computer to the physics of the problem, and you stop fighting nature and start harnessing it. That's where I think the next big leap in efficiency, and maybe in capability, is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response says physics-based hardware can use its natural dynamics to compute, with physical systems natively performing processes such as diffusion, Langevin sampling, and equilibration relevant to the models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the structure of the physical world and the structure of the hardware you're computing on don't have to be separate things. Right now we have this very roundabout pipeline: nature does something, we discretize it, we simulate it on digital hardware that's fundamentally built out of switches, and then we try to learn a representation of that simulation with a neural network. Every step in that chain is a lossy translation, and you pay for it in energy, in time, and in the inductive biases you accidentally bake in.

A physics-based accelerator, whether that's a thermodynamic system, an analog circuit, or a quantum device, is already natively doing the kind of computation you care about. If you want to sample from a Boltzmann distribution, you don't have to approximate it with a Markov chain on a GPU. You build a system whose equilibrium state is that distribution and you let it relax. The physics does the sampling for free. If you want to learn representations that respect conservation laws or symmetries or stochastic dynamics, it's a very natural idea to have the substrate itself obey those same laws, so the learned representation is sort of homomorphic to the thing being modeled.

So the fit is almost tautological in a way. Physics-informed representations are about encoding the priors of physics into your model. A physical computer has those priors built into its dynamics already. You're not fighting the hardware to express the structure you want, you're exploiting it. And there's a deeper point too, which is that the noise and dissipation that digital engineers spend enormous effort suppressing are actually resources for probabilistic learning. Nature is a very good random number generator and a very efficient optimizer. It seems a bit silly to spend gigawatts emulating that behavior with deterministic logic when you could just let the system be what it is.

r001.rationale: The response says a physics-based accelerator natively performs the relevant computation and that its physical dynamics can embody the same laws and priors the representation is meant to capture.

astra-6.text:
Well, the thing you’re trying to learn and the thing doing the computation can share a lot of the same structure. A physical system already evolves according to some dynamics. If those dynamics are relevant to the problem you care about, you can use them as part of the computation rather than having to simulate every step on a general-purpose processor.

And that gives you an inductive bias. Think about learning a representation that respects a symmetry or captures a conserved quantity. You could try to discover all of that from data, but if some of that structure is built into your model—and potentially into the physics of the device—you’re narrowing the search to representations that make physical sense.

The caveat is that the match matters. A device being physical doesn’t automatically make it useful for learning physics. You need to be able to encode the inputs, control or train the relevant parameters, and read out something useful without those costs overwhelming the advantage. But when there’s a good match, the physics becomes a computational resource and a source of structure for learning.

r001.rationale: The response says the physical system’s dynamics can be used as part of the computation when relevant, making the device’s physics a computational resource. This clearly conveys native execution of physics-informed programs as physical processes.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you think about what a physical system does, it evolves according to some underlying dynamics. And a lot of what we do in machine learning is spend computation simulating dynamics or learning structure that reflects the physical world. So there’s a natural question: can we use the dynamics of the hardware itself as part of the computation, rather than having to simulate every step digitally?

For example, if your hardware has particular symmetries or conservation laws, those can become an inductive bias for the model. You’re giving the learning system a structure that’s aligned with the phenomena you want it to represent. Ideally, that means it doesn’t have to rediscover all of that structure from data.

The caveat is that the match matters. A physical device isn’t automatically a useful learning machine. You still need to encode inputs, control the dynamics, read out useful quantities, and train the system efficiently. But when the physics of the device lines up with the structure of the problem, you have the possibility of getting both a useful representation and a more efficient way to compute it.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware dynamics can serve as part of the computation, instead of digitally simulating each step, which clearly conveys that the programs can execute natively as physical processes.
